chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Anbasa ibn Mus'ab, who said:

I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina, walking and riding. So I said to myself that I would ask him when I go over to him, but he initiated me with the hadith and said: 'Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to go out from his house walking when he pelted the Jamarah; and my house today is further than his house. So I ride until I get to his house. So when I arrive at his house, I walk until I pelt the Jamarah.'

key_terms.الْجَمْرَةَ: The Jamarah (the pillar or place of stoning)
key_terms.عَلِيَّ بْنَ الْحُسَيْنِ: Ali ibn Al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin), the fourth Imam
key_terms.مِنًى: Mina, a location near Mecca used during Hajj

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on riding versus walking during the stoning of the Jamarah in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Al-Sadiq (AS) illustrates the principle of *takhfif* (easing) in ritual practice by contrasting his own method of riding due to distance with the consistent walking of Imam Ali ibn Al-Husayn (AS), thereby highlighting that flexibility in Hajj rituals is rooted in the Sunnah of the Ahl al-Bayt. This narration serves as a practical legal precedent for allowing riders to dismount and walk for the final approach to the Jamarah, emphasizing that the spiritual merit lies in the intention and emulation of the Imams rather than rigid uniformity in mode of transport. It underscores the Shia scholarly view that the Imams' actions are the primary source of understanding the Prophet's Sunnah in its nuanced application.
